body.text: Foreign government officials often remark, with genuine puzzlement, that Japanese bureaucrats must never sleep. When a major announcement comes out of the United States in the morning, European counterparts have until close of business to begin formulating their response. Japan, by rights, should be asleep, yet its ministries are still awake, scrambling to keep up in real time. That agencies beyond the Ministry of Foreign Affairs manage to respond around the clock is, to outside observers, a genuine mystery.

Until the 1980s, working unlimited hours for unlimited output was considered a virtue in both the public and private sectors in Japan. But when the economic bubble burst in the early 1990s, the work ethic that had long been celebrated as the engine of Japan’s economic success suddenly became a target of criticism. Companies had their own incentive: cutting personnel costs, overtime pay included. And so Japan’s large private-sector firms moved rapidly to reform their working environments, shifting from “black” (exploitative) to “white” (employee-friendly).

The public sector was slower to change. Central government bureaucrats in particular had long signaled their competence to politicians and the public by shouldering ever-growing workloads with ever-fewer staff, an approach that had the effect of entrenching an abysmal working environment. The brutal conditions in the ministry district came to be satirized as “Black Kasumigaseki” — after the Tokyo neighborhood that houses the central bureaucracy — and talented university graduates began to turn away from government careers.

In the 2010s, the government began conducting its own employee engagement surveys of national civil servants. Academic researchers followed, carrying out a “Japanese Bureaucrats’ Survey” of six major ministries (Finance, Economy Trade and Industry, Internal Affairs and Communications, Land Infrastructure Transport and Tourism, Health Labor and Welfare, and Education Culture Sports Science and Technology) in 2019 and again in 2023. Some of the findings confirmed what many had suspected: that the workload borne by capable bureaucrats was fueling a strong intention to quit.

Three findings stood out. First, the sense of burden in day-to-day work had a powerful effect on intentions to resign. Administrative demand has grown and tasks have become more complex, while staffing was never adequate to begin with. When a colleague leaves, the burden on those remaining increases further, triggering a vicious cycle of additional departures.

Second, among the factors that most intensified the sense of overload, two stood out sharply: Diet affairs and legal risk. In Japan’s parliament, where government-opposition conflict tends to run hot, drafting answers for the prime minister’s office and the ministerial teams of each ministry, and preparing written responses to members’ parliamentary questions, carries the constant risk that a single misstep could precipitate a cabinet crisis. Opposition questions, moreover, are often submitted after the stated deadline as a negotiating tactic. And because the questions tend to be vague, bureaucrats must prepare exhaustive “anticipated Q&A” documents covering every conceivable scenario. The human cost of this was laid bare in a widely reported case: a young pregnant female official, working desperately until 3 a.m. to prepare documents for the following day’s Diet deliberations. On top of this, amendments to administrative litigation law have made lawsuits against the government more frequent, requiring ministries to consider litigation risk from the earliest stages of drafting legislation, an additional burden that weighs heavily on officials.

Third, however, the surveys also identified factors that reduce resignation intentions. Reducing workloads and raising salaries both help, though fiscal constraints make either difficult. But when a supervisor can clearly explain the content and significance of the work, or actively encourages new challenges, the desire to leave diminishes. It has long been understood that when a workplace environment can be improved to align organizational and individual goals, resignation intentions weaken accordingly.

The survey findings prompted the government to act. In 2025, hoping to attract talented new graduates, the government raised entry-level salaries substantially to a level closer to those at major private-sector firms. In 2026, salaries for officials in their early forties and on the cusp of promotion to division chief level were also raised significantly, to stem the flow of experienced bureaucrats to the private sector. While government pay still cannot match financial institutions or foreign-capital firms, working conditions are becoming increasingly comparable to those at large Japanese companies. Overtime in the workplace is now subject to limits; and ministries are beginning to define their organizational Mission, Vision, and Values, with supervisors expected to explain the rationale behind their instructions to junior staff.

That said, there are still areas where ministries cannot reform on their own, unlike private companies. The burden of responding to politicians — and of anticipating litigation risk — remains heavy. Above all, there are inherent limits to the extent to which public funds can be spent on improving pay and working conditions.

Reform has barely begun. For foreign government officials engaged in negotiations with Japan’s government or with its companies, it is worth paying close attention to the changes now quietly taking place among Japanese bureaucrats: officials who are, at long last, beginning to live something resembling a normal human life.
